newsitem.title: UK: Scientists say find gene for child cancer syndrome.
newsitem.headline: Scientists say find gene for child cancer syndrome.

text.p: Researchers working with mutant mice said on Wednesday they had found a gene they think could be responsible for Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which causes several kinds of childhood cancer.

Stephen Elledge of the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston and colleagues said they had tracked down a gene that, when mutated, caused a similar syndrome in mice they had deliberately bred to have a genetic mutation.
Reporting in the science journal Nature, they said this could mean the healthy version of the gene is one of a family of "tumour-suppressor" genes.

Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome affects one in every 13,700 births and 15 percent of cases run in families. Victims have a wide variety of growth abnormalities and their risk of cancer in childhood is 1,000 times above normal.

There had been evidence that the responsible gene was on chromosome 11. Elledge's team looked at a gene there that orders production of p57 KIP2, a protein that helps control cell growth and proliferation.
Mice bred to lack the ability to make the protein developed abdominal muscle defects, cleft palate and tumours -- the same symptoms as seen in human sufferers of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

The scientists said more study was needed, but their findings add to a growing body of knowledge indicating that several interacting systems work to keep the body in order and prevent the out-of-control cell proliferation that marks cancer.
